title: Registration
text:
Registration for the EarthCODE Hackathon 2026 is now open. Register here!

Information for applicants
The EarthCODE Hackathon will be held from November 30 to December 4, 2026 at ESA ESRIN, Frascati, Italy. The event will provide an opportunity to bring the communities who are using EarthCODE tools and services as close as possible to the people who are building them.
We welcome applications from:

Members of ESA Science Clusters, particularly addressing: Ocean, Carbon and Polar science communities.
Earth system scientists working with Earth Observation (EO) data who want to create, reuse, or publish data collections.

We especially invite early career researchers, PhD students, and post-docs!
To best benefit from the event, we recommend some familiarity or experience with:

Earth Observation (EO) data (especially from Polar, Carbon, and Ocean Clusters, including interdisciplinary applications)
Programming skills using Python. We plan to accept participants with broad skill levels and backgrounds in programming. However, to best benefit from and contribute to the program, some experience with Python, R, or a similar programming language is recommended.
Familiarity with Git and GitHub would be beneficial, but not required. We will provide a short tutorial on Git and GitHub during the hackathon.

Please note that if there are more applicants than we have space, priority will be given to people who work with the ESA Polar Cluster, Ocean Cluster, Carbon Cluster, ScienceHub, Phi Lab, and people who work with ESA data.
Questions? Send us an email.


Application
In the application form, we encourage you to think about and provide a science use case that you would like to prototype or work on. At the beginning of the hackathon, participants will be able to pitch their use case to support the formation of projects, and participants will form teams based on shared interests.
We are able to provide some needs-based travel support for participants who require it.
Applications will close on October 30, 2026. Accepted applicants will be notified no later than November 4, 2026. We expect to accommodate approximately 40-60 participants.
We have provided the registration questions below so that you can think about your answers before you start the application process.

title: Hackathon Roles
text: There are many roles required to envision, organize, and execute a successful hackathon. The roles described here are lightly modified from those outlined in the eScience Hackweek Guide. Some roles, such as Community Lead, Technical Leads, and Tutorial Leads are heavily involved in the planning stages, and are fulfilled by multiple people on the organizing team. Other roles are established and become very hands-on during the ESA EarthCODE Hackathon itself.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Community Lead (ESA + Openscapes)
The Community Lead guides the activities of community members engaged in hackathon organization and execution.

Goals

Matching the technical and scientific needs of the community to the design of this hackathon.
Ensuring everyone involved is sufficiently resourced to carry out the work.
Strategizing on how best to implement practices of open-source science within this community.
Building supportive partnerships and communities of practice before, during, and after the hackathon.



Specific Activities

Work with the community to define the overarching goals of the hackathon.
Build a diverse, inclusive, and equitable hackathon organizing team; recruit broadly for organizers and participants.
Help organize and attend event planning meetings.
Review tutorial content, evaluating meeting hackathon goals, learning objectives, and community relevance.
Attend the hackathon and be available to assist with project and tutorial work.
Facilitate and/or lead longer-term community efforts to build on collaborations fostered around the hackathon.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Technical Lead (Lampata + Openscapes)
The Technical Lead is experienced with the computational platforms that support collaboration and learning during the hackathon.

Goals

Empowering hackathon organizers to follow best practices in creating open source learning materials.
Ensuring shared hackathon tools are accessible to everyone.
Guiding workflow development to be reproducible and deployable on multiple infrastructures.



Specific Activities

Set up a shared computational environment.
Deploy the hackathon website.
Teach hackathon organizers how to use GitHub and the shared computational environment for planning and design of the hackathon.
Assist tutorial leads in uploading their notebooks and sample datasets.
Help participants gain access to shared resources.
Archive hackathon outcomes.
Provide consultation on computational needs that evolve after the hackathon.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Tutorial Leads
Tutorial Leads use their knowledge of data science tools and methods to create online learning materials and teach tutorials during the hackathon. See the Instructor Guide for guidance.

Goals

Fostering the learning and development of community members on topics of interest at the hackathon.
Supporting the design of a shared open source curriculum.



Specific Activities

Define learning outcomes that are tailored to community needs.
Build new skills in data science pedagogy.
Offer feedback to peers on tutorial design.
Create interactive tutorials in Jupyter Notebooks.
Use GitHub to share tutorial content in an open source environment.
Teach or assist with teaching tutorials during the hackathon.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Project Consultant (Cluster Leads / Representatives)
The Project Consultant has a big-picture view of the possible scope of projects for the hackathon community, and helps participants get clear on project ideas and objectives. See the Project Guide for more information on projects, and the Mentor Guide for guidance on mentoring teams, as project consultants will also play this role.

Goals

Communicating the purpose and approach of small group collaborations.
Shaping community ideas into well-defined and realistic project designs.
Creating a welcoming space for participants to engage in project ideation and completion.



Specific Activities

Present session to participants about the goals and scope of hackathon projects.
Suggest project ideas.
Encourage participants to pitch project ideas before the hackathon.
Assemble and make sense of project ideas.
Guide the formation of project teams on the first day of the hackathon.
Facilitate small group collaborations during the hackathon.
Assist teams in setting goals and sharing results.
Provide guidance to teams who wish to remain connected after the hackathon.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Project Leads
Project Leads have an interest in guiding small teams in their progress toward hackathon project goals. Usually the project lead is the person who pitches a project idea.

Goals

Supporting all team members in getting something valuable out of their time during hackathon project work.
Fostering collaboration within a small team.
Laying the foundation for long-term project development after the hackathon is complete.



Specific Activities

Pitch an idea for a project.
Gather a team and help each person get clear on their individual goals during the project work.
Facilitate relationship-building and development of collaborative structures among the team.
Help everyone design project work that is within the scope of this hackathon.
Lead daily standup team check-ins.

title: Hackathon Roles
text:
Mentor / Helper
Mentors and Helpers have knowledge of data or domain science tools and methods that they wish to share with their peers, or they may have facilitation skills to help keep project teams well-scoped, organized, and inclusive. They can include ESA staff, community members and hackathon participants. See the Mentor Guide for more guidance.

Goals

Helping hackathon participants move past stuck points and complete learning objectives.
Including all participants in the learning process.
Empowering learners to connect with external educational resources.



Specific Activities

Answer questions from participants during the teaching of tutorials.
Help participants access resources needed to address specific problems.
Participate in project teams and assist with technical questions.
Offer feedback to tutorial developers based on participant experiences with the materials.

title: Projects Overview
text: Collaborative projects are a key component of the ESA EarthCODE Hackathon, in which you get to interact with others closely and apply new skills to make something exciting happen: it can be creating tools to streamline access to a particular data source, creating and visualizing new, integrated datasets, testing existing models with new data sources, or anything else you may want to do at the intersection of earth and data science.

title: Projects Overview
text:
Tips for getting started

Potentially choose something that you’ve been interested in but haven’t had the time or skills to do before, or something you can continue to work on post Hackathon.
Hacking is a community activity! It’s okay to choose projects that you can’t accomplish alone as other people will be there to help you, both at the Hackathon and outside of it!
Help your group members: you might be the person they need to solve their problem, and vice versa.
When discussing, pitch your explanation to the least experienced people in the group, and you’ll end up better understanding what you’re trying to do, or need to revise your idea.
You can mix programming languages as needed in order to get started, but do check in with your project mentors and group members to make sure your efforts are straightforward to be absorbed into the project.

title: Projects Overview
text:
What is a Hack?
A “hack” is a small project that aims to solve a specific problem using computational tools.
Examples of hacks include:

Creation of new datasets from existing data sources
Build a working demo of a new or modified algorithm
Outline of a larger project, with some key features scoped
Visualization of an old dataset in a new manner
Modify an algorithm and apply it to a new dataset
Combine two pre-existing pieces of code to perform some new function
Create a tool to apply to work with existing code, datasets
Transform code from one language to another to use with other tools
Update old code to run faster, on new machines, and/or more efficiently
Extend an existing project with an additional feature

title: Projects Overview
section: Why hack at the ESA EarthCODE Hackathon?
text:
Why hack at the ESA EarthCODE Hackathon?
Increasingly, research and software development are conducted by groups of people with diverse skills and backgrounds. We believe this collaborative work leads to more innovative solutions to complex problems. At the ESA EarthCODE Hackathon, our goal is to explore with you some of the skills needed to navigate technical and social challenges of working in these kinds of collaborative settings. We believe the best way to do so is to provide opportunities for you to gain hands-on experience in working together with others on a well-defined problem related to earth sciences.

title: Projects Overview
section: How will the projects be conducted?
text:
How will the projects be conducted?

On day 1 we will facilitate the sharing of ideas and begin formation of people into small teams (2-5 people)
Once formed, each team will narrow in on a set of tasks and create and present a one-slide “Project Pitch”. Teams will then be able to refine their project ideas based on feedback from the other teams and mentors.
Teams will work together on their projects for the remainder of the Hackathon, with mentors available to provide guidance and support.
In the afternoon of day 4, each team will present their work to the other teams and mentors. Presentations will be informal and will focus on what was accomplished, what was learned, and what the next steps are for the project.
The morning of day 5 will have time for teams to meet and decide on post-hackathon plans and give “pop-up” presentations if they want.

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
Please specify the target audience for this tutorial. What does the audience need to know to be able to benefit from your tutorial? Can you eliminate unnecessary prerequisites?
Hackathon participants come from diverse technical backgrounds: while some may have basic scripting experience, others may have built complex applications within their domain, and still may be completely unfamiliar with libraries used in an adjacent domain.

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
Please specify the target audience for this tutorial. What does the audience need to know to be able to benefit from your tutorial? Can you eliminate unnecessary prerequisites?
Hackathon participants come from diverse technical backgrounds: while some may have basic scripting experience, others may have built complex applications within their domain, and still may be completely unfamiliar with libraries used in an adjacent domain.

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
Learning Objectives
Please provide a few measurable learning objectives for your tutorial: those should be short statements of what participants will be able to do immediately after the tutorial. Consider learning objectives of varying complexity: some expect participants to be able to execute simple tasks, while others expect them to be able to develop new approaches to address a problem. You can use the Bloom’s Taxonomy categorization to structure your objectives.
Example:
After the lesson the learners will be able to * Outline elements of ML pipelines * List major differences between types of ML methods, and steps to proceed to evaluate their performance * Identify contexts where deep learning can be useful * Organize labeled datasets in a format expected by ML libraries
Think about the balance of how your tutorial can be helpful to participants during the hackathon vs. afterwards throughout their careers.

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
General Tips
Think of ways to engage the audience during the tutorial. That can also set the right tone of how much detail you need to provide. Remember the more experienced participants may be the more vocal ones so think of ways to hear from everybody without making them feel uncomfortable for not knowing a concept.
Although the content of your tutorial may not seem a lot when presented as stand-alone, the participants are going through a sequence of tutorials during the week, and are also learning a lot of new things for their projects.

If using notebooks/code, be explicit whether you expect people to follow along running the cells/changing code on the fly, or they can just follow your demo, and dive into the notebook later.
Scrolling through notebooks/code can become pretty confusing, so consider having sections in the notebook and hiding the code cells, only to reveal it when talking about a specific section
Add a few key points after a section
If there are steps for which participants need to navigate to specific places on a website, consider saving snapshots and circling the places they need to click to avoid them missing crucial steps after which they cannot navigate the lesson; pause to make sure people are at the right place
Look through the tutorial and see what jargon/acronyms you are using:

Remove the ones not crucial for the tutorial
Spell out the ones that the participants need to know
If some are not important, be explicit that they are not important right now, and they are just there for future reference

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
Tips for Use Case/Workflow Presentations

While preparing your presentation, identify which of its components generalize outside of the use case; state those explicitly to help listeners focus on what can be relevant to them
Share lessons learned: what worked well, what did not
Did you have to pivot the project?

title: Tutorial Instructor Guide
text:
Technical Setup
The hackathon will provide a JupyterHub environment in EarthCODE, within which participants can run any interactive tutorials. As an instructor you will have to ensure that your tutorial can run within the environment. For that you will need to:

Talk to the organizing team to get added to JupyterHub
Familiarize yourself with the JupyterHub environment
Identify which packages (and corresponding versions) you will need for the tutorial and provide them to the organizing team so that they are included into an image for building the JupyterHub (those can be PyPi, conda/conda-forge, R)
Contribute your tutorial content to the tutorials repo (link TBD)
Ensure participants have access to the datasets used in the tutorial

If there is need to store some datasets on JupyterHub, let us know!
Make sure the datasets are reduced to a reasonable size to demonstrate the point, but not make the tutorial cumbersome to run
If the tutorial requires executing many expensive queries to a server, please, consider storing a local copy for the demonstration

title: EarthCODE Hackathon 2026
text:
About
We are developing the shape and schedule of the hackathon in the open, and this website will be updated as we go. Please check back for updates!
The EarthCODE Hackathon will take place from 30 November – 4 December 2026 at ESA ESRIN, in Frascati, Italy. The event will provide an opportunity to bring the communities who are using EarthCODE tools and services as close as possible to the people who are building them.
The EarthCODE Hackathon will bring together Ocean, Carbon, and Polar scientists, experts in FAIR data and reproducible workflows and open source developers to focus on the creation and enhancement of analysis ready data collections.
The goals of the hackathon are to:

Demonstrate how EarthCODE services support the publication and reuse of scientific data from ESA Science Clusters
Enable learning and knowledge transfer of modern data science tools and workflows for Earth system scientists.
Promote open access and visibility of high impact scientific datasets via dashboards and interactive viewers
Foster collaboration between scientists and the open source developer community
Contribute to the evolution of EarthCODE services and tools

Hackathons are participant-driven events that strive to create welcoming spaces for participants to learn new things, build community and gain hands-on experience with collaboration and team science. During EarthCODE Hackathon 2026, we will have a combination of science lectures, coding tutorials, and group projects (pitched and chosen by participants).

Registration
See the registration page for more information on how to apply. We are able to provide some needs-based travel support. We welcome applications from:

Members of ESA Science Clusters, particularly addressing: Ocean, Carbon and Polar science communities.
Earth system scientists working with Earth Observation (EO) data who want to create, reuse, or publish data collections. Polar science communities.

We especially invite early career researchers, PhD students, and post-docs!
Questions? Send us an email.

title: Logistics
text:
Event Facility
The hackathon will be held at ESA ESRIN in Frascati, a small town 20km south of Rome, Italy. Power supply and WiFi access will be available at the venue. If you have non-European power plugs, please bring an appropriate adapter.

Compute
Please bring your own laptop to work on at the hackathon. You will have access to the EarthCODE compute platform, which is a cloud-based environment for running Jupyter notebooks and other tools.

title: Logistics
text:
Transportation
Travel to and from Frascati is the responsibility of the participants. The closest international airport is Rome Fiumicino (FCO), which is approximately 50km from Frascati. See Getting to ESRIN for more information on how to get to Frascati from Rome. Some travel support is available, and will be provided on a case-by-case basis. See the registration page for more information.

Daily Courtesy Transport
The ESRIN facility is located approximately 2.5km outside Frascati. There will be a courtesy bus to take participants from Frascati to ESRIN in the morning and back to Frascati in the afternoon each day of the hackathon. The pick-up and drop-off point will be at Piazza Guglielmo Marconi.

text:
Food
Lunch and a morning and afternoon snack/coffee will be served each day at the ESRIN canteen. On the evening of the first day, we will have an Icebreaker event at the ESRIN canteen, with non-alcoholic drinks and snacks provided. Breakfast and dinner are not provided.

title: Frequently Asked Questions
text:
Applying

What background or skills do I need?
We plan to accept participants with broad skill levels and backgrounds. Some experience with Python, R, or a similar programming language is recommended, as is some familiarity with Earth Observation data. Familiarity with Git and GitHub is beneficial but not required, since we will provide a short tutorial during the hackathon.


Do I need to come with a project or team?
No, however we encourage you to think of a science use case you would like to work on, and you will have an opportunity to pitch it at the start of the hackathon. Participants then form small project teams (ideally 3-5 people per team) based on shared interests and goals. ESA Cluster leads will also have suggestions for potential projects.


Can I join the hackathon remotely?
The hackathon is an in-person-only event at ESA ESRIN in Frascati, Italy, and applicants are asked to confirm that they can attend in person for the full week.


Are applicants affiliated with institutions outside ESA Member States eligible to participate in the hackathon?
Applicants from institutions outside ESA Member States are eligible to participate. If we reach capacity, priority will be given to people participating in relevant projects as part of the ESA Science Clusters or the Earth System Science Initiative.


When will I find out if I have been selected?
Applications close on October 30, 2026, and accepted applicants will be notified no later than November 4, 2026.



Cost and travel support

Is there a cost to attend, and are meals included?
There is no fee for the hackathon itself. Participants are responsible for their own travel and accommodation, with some travel support available. Morning and afternoon snacks and coffee will be provided each day, along with an Icebreaker event on the evening of the first day. Lunch is available for you to purchase at the ESA canteen each day; breakfast and dinner are not provided. See the logistics page for details.


How does financial assistance work? If travel support is available, what does it typically cover?
We are able to offer needs-based travel support to a number of participants up to a maximum amount that will be reimbursed after the event - this is designed to cover typical travel and accommodation expenses for people traveling within Europe. Please describe your needs in the registration form when applying. Selected participants will be informed before they are required to confirm attendance.


Is the needs-based travel support available to all participants, or is it restricted to applicants from Member States?
Funding for travel support is only eligible for applicants from organizations or institutions in ESA Member States.



Preparing to attend

Does on-site access to ESRIN require any additional administrative steps?
Yes, access to the ESRIN site is subject to security verifications. More information on what this looks like will be shared with selected participants.


Do I need to bring my own laptop?
Yes, please bring your own laptop. You will have access to the EarthCODE compute platform, a cloud-based environment for running Jupyter notebooks and other tools. See the logistics page for details.


Do you have accommodation recommendations?
Yes, please see the logistics page for recommendations.

title: Project Mentor Guide
text:
A project mentor can also propose a project idea and lead it. But the priority should be on enabling leadership and collaborative work by participants themselves. The project mentor shouldn’t be the center of attention.
Monitor participation by everyone, to mitigate situations where extroverts dominate discussions or introverts don’t feel comfortable to participate. Suggest ways to rebalance participation so that everyone feels they have something to contribute.
Provide scientific advisory support. Serve as a resource. Ideally the project will be in your broader scientific domains, but it’s not really necessary.
Provide technical advisory support. Serve as a resource for Python, R, git/GitHub, sources of relevant data, analytical or data processing methods, etc. Help the team arrive at solutions to specific challenges.
When you can’t help directly, help them seek help elsewhere in the ESA EarthCODE community. Link to other helpers or participants who may have relevant expertise.
Maintain regular communication with project team via a Slack channel, in person (as appropriate) and GitHub issues and PR discussions.
Be a resource for the preparation of project presentations. Make suggestions if the team is stuck because the different strands of a project are not coming together semi cleanly.

title: Tutorial Helpers
text:

Ask tutorial presenter ahead of time if:

they would like to answer questions throughout the tutorial, or hold questions until the end
they would like the moderator to ask the questions from Slack, or read the questions on Slack themselves

Remind participants to add questions to the tutorials Slack channel and to upvote questions they want answered
Introduce the tutorial and tutorial presenter
Ask questions (if requested by the presenter) that have the most +1 reactions
Add a ✅ to Q&A questions answered on Slack
Add a 🔥 to burning Q&A questions that should be answered by presenter (not needed if moderator reads out questions for the presenter)
Keep track of time and end session on time
